meetings.label: Meeting A — March 12, 2027

speakers.name: Dr. Lucía Herrera
speakers.background: A forest ecologist with six years of postdoctoral and field-research experience in tropical dry-forest and forest-frontier landscapes in Latin America. She designs carbon-monitoring studies using permanent forest inventory plots, biomass allometry, Landsat and Sentinel time series, and spatial analyses of leakage and disturbance. She has contributed to evaluations of avoided-deforestation projects but is wary of claims that remote sensing alone can establish causality or long-term permanence.
speakers.distinct_perspective: Lucía treats the proposed credits first as an empirical claim about biophysical change: compared with a defensible counterfactual, did the program prevent carbon loss, and did clearing shift beyond the project boundary? She will press for transparent baseline construction, field validation of satellite classifications, and monitoring that distinguishes temporary canopy retention from durable carbon storage. She is cautious about governance analyses that infer ecological outcomes from stated rules without measuring forest change.
speakers.language_complexity: moderate — balances jargon with accessible language

speakers.name: Dr. Samuel Okoro
speakers.background: A political scientist with four years of postdoctoral research on decentralization, land tenure, and environmental enforcement in rural resource-governance settings. His work combines institutional mapping, elite and household interviews, archival review of concessions and cadastral records, and comparative case analysis. He has studied how formally designated conservation authority is altered by overlapping customary claims, patronage networks, and uneven enforcement capacity.
speakers.distinct_perspective: Samuel approaches Alto Verde as a contested authority system rather than a bounded project site. He wants to identify who can credibly authorize land-use restrictions, how municipal offices and village councils resolve—or fail to resolve—overlapping claims, and whether enforcement changes incentives for residents, migrants, and outside logging interests. He sees forest outcomes and credit durability as contingent on legitimacy, enforcement capacity, and distributional conflict, while remaining willing to revise his account in light of ecological evidence and local testimony.
speakers.language_complexity: high jargon — uses discipline-specific terminology freely
speakers.epistemic_stance: open to other perspectives, willing to revise

speakers.name: Maya Srinivasan
speakers.background: A fourth-year PhD student in science and technology studies researching carbon-accounting infrastructures and environmental certification. She has conducted ethnographic observation of verification processes, interviews with project developers and auditors, and document analysis of methodologies, monitoring reports, maps, and registry records. Her dissertation examines how categories such as forest, baseline, additionality, and local participation become stabilized across field teams, software platforms, and certification institutions.
speakers.distinct_perspective: Maya examines how measurements and assumptions acquire authority as tradable credits. She will ask how plot measurements, satellite classifications, boundary maps, and baseline models are translated into audit-ready evidence; who gets to classify uncertainty as acceptable; and why some local accounts of land use or boundaries count as data while others are treated as anecdote. She does not deny the importance of ecological measurement or institutional analysis, but emphasizes that the credit is produced through practices of standardization, verification, and admissibility that deserve study in their own right.
speakers.language_complexity: moderate — balances jargon with accessible language
speakers.epistemic_stance: defers to other experts outside their domain

transcript.speaker: Dr. Samuel Okoro
transcript.text: Morning, everyone. Before we start, did the updated municipal concession file from last week ever come through to the group? I may have missed it. For today, I was hoping we could- I want us to get clear on what each of us needs before we treat the proposed project boundary as meaningful, instead of just taking the designation at face value.

transcript.speaker: Maya Srinivasan
transcript.text: I don't think I saw the updated concession file either—was it meant to include the GIS attachment, or just the municipal resolution? For me, the boundary becomes meaningful partly through the paperwork that makes it auditable. Which map version is treated as controlling, who signed off on it, and whether residents' boundary accounts can enter the record as more than, sorry, just context.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Samuel Okoro
transcript.text: Mm, yes, that distinction matters.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Lucía Herrera
transcript.text: Quick question from last week, did anyone ever circulate the preliminary GIS layer with the concession file? On the ecological side, I need to know which boundary is operational before we build any baseline or leakage analysis. A legally clean polygon can still be pretty meaningless if clearing and local access patterns, if they just ignore it.

transcript.speaker: Maya Srinivasan
transcript.text: Before we settle on an operational polygon, do we know which certification methodology and verifier Alto Verde is likely to use? I'm asking because the admissible map, and even what counts as a discrepancy worth documenting- that can change with their rules, not just with what's happening on the ground.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Lucía Herrera
transcript.text: I’d want to avoid letting the verifier’s preferred polygon quietly become our ecological, um, unit. Do we know whether they’ve named a methodology yet? Because if not, we should probably preserve the competing boundary versions and test leakage across a wider surrounding zone, rather than only just outside whichever line ends up in the documents.

transcript.speaker: Maya Srinivasan
transcript.text: Preserving them is important, but I'd also want us to record when one version starts being treated as authoritative and who is doing that. A wider zone may capture leakage ecologically, but if the methodology only recognizes the project polygon, it can- that gap can disappear from the credit file, and that's something we should follow too.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Lucía Herrera
transcript.text: Mm, yes, and that gap isn't just administrative for us. If the recognized polygon is narrower than the area where access restrictions or land prices are changing, we could call the project stable while carbon loss has simply shifted—moved. Do Samuel's interviews or records show who actually recognizes these different lines when the formal map and local claims diverge?

transcript.speaker: Dr. Samuel Okoro
transcript.text: Not yet, at least not systematically. The cadastral review has already turned up one awkward case. Two adjacent parcels show up as a single municipal concession, but village notes describe them as separately managed commons. So I'd want to interview council members, municipal land staff, and users around those parcels before we infer recognition from the map. It could be an obsolete record, but it could also be a deliberately useful ambiguity.

transcript.speaker: Maya Srinivasan
transcript.text: That’s exactly the kind of ambiguity I’d want to trace, not resolve too quickly. Samuel, if the municipal staff and the councils give incompatible accounts, what would persuade you that one is actually shaping land-use decisions? Use patterns, sanctions, who grants permission? And we should keep the contradictory records in the file, not just turn them into one clean boundary.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Lucía Herrera
transcript.text: Mm, sanctions especially.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Samuel Okoro
transcript.text: Sanctions are one indicator, but not the only one. Who can authorize cultivation or timber access, whether people comply with that authorization, and who residents turn to when there's a dispute may tell us more than a formal penalty. The awkward part is that patronage can make a municipal claim look effective in one household network and irrelevant in the next, so we should ask about actual episodes, not just stated rules.

transcript.speaker: Maya Srinivasan
transcript.text: Actual episodes seem crucial because those are also the moments when a verifier may ask for evidence and decide whose account is legible. I’m wondering, if a household follows a council’s permission informally but the municipal file says otherwise, what record would make that practice visible without- without immediately recoding it as anecdotal?

transcript.speaker: Dr. Lucía Herrera
transcript.text: Could we geo-reference those episodes, even roughly? Where permission was granted, where cultivation actually occurred, and when. I’m not saying that makes an account more- it doesn’t make it more true, but it would let us compare the accounts against the disturbance record and see whether those apparently stable pixels are tied to a boundary people actually use.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Samuel Okoro
transcript.text: Mm, roughly, yes.

transcript.speaker: Maya Srinivasan
transcript.text: That would help, especially if we keep the rough location and the account linked, rather than stripping the account away once it becomes a point on a map. Lucía, what would make you doubt the satellite classification, even if it clears the usual accuracy threshold? Say residents describe seasonal cultivation or access that the imagery is, is flattening out.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Lucía Herrera
transcript.text: I’d doubt it if the classification is just seeing a green canopy signal and not the structure underneath. In the dry-forest pilot, we had plots that looked similarly stable from space but had very different stem density and regrowth, so seasonal cultivation or repeated understory clearing could matter a lot, even above the nominal accuracy threshold. We’d need a few field plots and, ideally, dates from those local accounts to see what the sensor is actually- what it’s missing.

transcript.speaker: Maya Srinivasan
transcript.text: And I’d want the field notes to say not just what the plot shows, but what prompted us to put a plot there, there. A local account, a classification edge, a suspected access route. Otherwise, by the time it reaches a monitoring report, the plot can look like neutral validation instead of a response to a dispute about what the imagery is seeing.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Lucía Herrera
transcript.text: Yeah, keep that provenance.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Samuel Okoro
transcript.text: And for the permission episodes, the provenance includes who felt able to speak to us at all. If we sample only people named by the council or municipal office, we may reproduce the same authority claim we're trying to examine. I think we need a way to reach recent migrants and households along the, um, access routes too.

transcript.speaker: Maya Srinivasan
transcript.text: I’d be careful that our recruitment trail becomes part of the evidence record, who referred whom, which accounts we couldn’t reach, and why. Otherwise, an audit later might read the interview set as a neutral community consultation, when it was already shaped by the same access routes and authorities we’re trying to—

transcript.speaker: Dr. Samuel Okoro
transcript.text: And I'd add a small safeguard. Recruitment through offices and councils should be just one entry point, not the frame. We can sample outward from the disputed parcels and access routes, then record refusals and referral chains separately, separately, because otherwise silence from migrants or unregistered users gets mistaken for absence of a claim.

transcript.speaker: Maya Srinivasan
transcript.text: Yes, and that separate record matters for more than recruitment ethics. If the project documents end up saying "community consultation," we should be able to see which people and claims were excluded by the route into consultation, instead of letting that label stand in for a settled constituency. And I'm still wondering, before field preparation starts, whether we can get the methodology and verifier name. I lost the thread there, but that's what I mean.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Samuel Okoro
transcript.text: I haven’t seen it named, no. Before field preparation, could we get the sponsor to confirm both the proposed methodology and verifier, but not let that determine our sampling frame? I’m still concerned the municipal files may be outdated, so I’d rather preserve the competing, competing claims even if the eventual credit documentation only recognizes one polygon.

transcript.speaker: Maya Srinivasan
transcript.text: I think we should ask the sponsor for those names now, but frame it as a documentation question, not as though their eventual choice is the ground truth. And if they can't name them yet, that uncertainty is worth recording too, because the evidence standards may still be getting, um, negotiated while the boundary is already being made operational.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Lucía Herrera
transcript.text: Alongside that request, I think we should ask whether there are actually comparable reference areas, and whether there’s enough historical imagery to build a baseline before anyone implies the credits are measurable. If the baseline is weak, knowing the eventual verifier helps us understand the paperwork, but it won’t make avoided loss identifiable. I need to check the, um, archive coverage around Alto Verde, though.

transcript.speaker: Maya Srinivasan
transcript.text: Mm, and if the baseline has to be revised because the archive or the reference areas are inadequate, I’d want to follow how that revision gets documented. Whether it shows up as a technical limitation, a methodological choice, or it just—whether it disappears before the credit claim. We should ask the sponsor for any early baseline memos, if they exist, along with the methodology and verifier.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Lucía Herrera
transcript.text: Hm, if they exist.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Samuel Okoro
transcript.text: And I’d want any early baseline memo read alongside the access history, not just as a technical precursor. A reference area may look comparable in the imagery but sit under a quite different enforcement arrangement or set of claims, and that changes what displacement would mean. We can probably keep that as an open check until Lucía knows what coverage is available.

transcript.speaker: Maya Srinivasan
transcript.text: Before we break, could the sponsor request explicitly include any correspondence about why particular reference areas were selected or rejected? The final baseline memo may make those choices look settled, and I think the earlier exchanges are where we may actually see what kinds of ecological and governance differences were treated as- what they treated as material.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Samuel Okoro
transcript.text: Yes—especially the rejected reference areas; those choices may encode governance differences.

transcript.speaker: Maya Srinivasan
transcript.text: I think we should let people go a few minutes early. Thanks, both. Once we hear back from the sponsor and Lucía has checked the coverage, we can pick this up.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Samuel Okoro
transcript.text: All right. Take care, both.

meetings.label: Meeting B — March 19, 2027

speakers.name: Dr. Maya Serrano
speakers.background: Dr. Serrano is a cognitive neuroscientist with 12 years of research experience studying human spatial learning and episodic memory. She designs behavioral tasks that pair navigation or object-location learning with post-learning rest, then relates later recall accuracy and confidence to hippocampal activity measured with intracranial recordings and high-resolution fMRI. Her recent work has focused on distinguishing neural signatures associated with durable memory from activity that accompanies weak or forgotten experiences.
speakers.distinct_perspective: She begins with the behavioral phenomenon: what was learned, what is later remembered, and whether a putative replay event predicts a meaningful memory outcome. For the proposed study, she advocates a spatial-memory task followed by quiet rest and a delayed recall test, with preregistered criteria separating stronger memories from forgetting. She treats hippocampal place representations and replay as mechanisms that must be anchored to interpretable changes in memory behavior, while recognizing that the exact neural readout requires close collaboration with computational modeling.
speakers.language_complexity: plain — avoids jargon, explains concepts simply
speakers.epistemic_stance: uncertain about how their methods apply to this problem

speakers.name: Dr. Aaron Feldman
speakers.background: Dr. Feldman is a computational neuroscientist and principal investigator with 15 years of experience analyzing multichannel hippocampal recordings in rodents and humans. His lab develops Bayesian decoders, state-space models, and generative simulations of sequential neural activity to study candidate replay during rest and sleep. He has published methodological work on false-positive sequence detection, including how classifier calibration, temporal smoothing, and threshold selection can turn noisy population activity into apparently structured replay events.
speakers.distinct_perspective: He frames replay as an inference problem: candidate sequences must be decoded from population activity, tested against carefully matched nulls, and compared with explicit models of sequence generation rather than accepted because they resemble trajectories. He supports linking neural events to later recall, but emphasizes that behavioral associations cannot rescue a biased detector. He will push the group to preregister decoder training, classifier thresholds, null distributions, and neural inclusion criteria, while leaving open which model-comparison metric—such as predictive likelihood, Bayes factors, or cross-validated performance—should be primary.
speakers.language_complexity: moderate — balances jargon with accessible language
speakers.epistemic_stance: defers to other experts outside their domain

transcript.speaker: Dr. Aaron Feldman
transcript.text: Hi Maya—quick logistical thing, did the revised task timeline I sent after last week ever come through? I mainly want us to leave today with a sensible recall endpoint and an analysis plan that doesn't let the replay detector decide the result for us.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Serrano
transcript.text: It did. Sorry, I only got to it this morning. I like the delayed recall endpoint, but before we lock it in, do you think the timing gives us enough variation to separate accurate location memory from confident-but-wrong routes? That showed up in the pilot, and I don't want confidence to quietly become the outcome just because it's easier to score.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Aaron Feldman
transcript.text: Confidence has to stay separate from accuracy. Otherwise, we risk calling a vivid reconstruction a durable spatial memory. From the neural side, I'd prefer exact location as the primary endpoint, and then model route structure and confidence alongside it. But how much forgetting did the pilot actually show at that delay? We need enough errors to discriminate outcomes without making the layout feel arbitrary.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Serrano
transcript.text: In the pilot, at that delay, we had enough wrong locations to work with, but not enough outright blanks for a clean remembered-versus-forgotten split. So I'd keep exact location as the primary outcome, but preregister graded accuracy instead of forcing a binary label. Maybe we add a slightly longer delayed test for a subset. I worry the layout gets arbitrary if we just increase the difficulty.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Aaron Feldman
transcript.text: A subset could be useful, though I’d worry about turning delay into a second task condition when we have too little data per cell. If we keep graded location error as primary, could we make the longer test exploratory at first? And for the recordings, I need to check the unit yield. I mean, whether it supports item-level decoding across both delays before we build the neural question around that split.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Serrano
transcript.text: Exploratory makes sense for the longer delay. I don't want the primary question to depend on a sparse subgroup. But before we settle that, how stable are your place estimates from learning into quiet rest? If the decoder itself shifts across those periods, then an item-level replay difference by graded accuracy is hard to interpret, even if we have enough trials.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Aaron Feldman
transcript.text: That’s the right concern. I wouldn’t assume the learning-place fields transfer unchanged into rest. We need to quantify cross-period stability on held-out learning data, and probably allow an explicit remapping or drift component instead of baking stability into the decoder. If rest decoding only looks item-specific under one smoothing window or one registration choice, then, um, that’s a detector result, not evidence for replay.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Serrano
transcript.text: And could you send me the null checks you used in the earlier sequential analyses? I’m especially interested in which matched controls actually produced convincing-looking sequences, time shuffles, trajectory-label swaps, whatever, because I’d want those specified alongside the drift model before we ask whether a rest event predicts lower location error.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Aaron Feldman
transcript.text: The most deceptive ones were usually the label swaps and rate-matched population surrogates. Simple time shuffles can be almost too easy to reject because they wreck the autocorrelation. I’ll send the full set, but I think we should preregister at least a trajectory-label permutation, a within-rest circular shift, and simulations with drift but no sequential generator. Otherwise the drift model is just another way for the decoder to manufacture—

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Serrano
transcript.text: The drift-only simulations feel essential, because otherwise we could end up explaining a behavioral association with a sequence score that the rest data could generate on its own. I’d want the same nulls applied within the graded accuracy analysis, not just to establish that replay exists overall. And maybe we should decide now whether confidence is a covariate or a secondary outcome, since those, those confident spatial errors were pretty systematic in the pilot.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Aaron Feldman
transcript.text: I'd make confidence a secondary outcome, not a covariate in the primary graded-error model. It may be part of the mechanism, or at least share variance with whatever replay is doing, so controlling for it up front could erase the association we actually need to understand. We can preregister a sensitivity model with confidence included, and ask whether the neural effect is specific to location error or tracks, um, subjective certainty too.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Serrano
transcript.text: I think that’s the cleanest split. The primary model is replay versus graded location error, and then confidence is secondary, and the sensitivity model tells us whether the apparent spatial effect survives once certainty is in there. I’d also like to look at the confident-wrong cases descriptively. They may be few, but they’re exactly where a replay account could mean something different.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Aaron Feldman
transcript.text: Descriptively is right for those, and I'd be very cautious about making them a separate neural subgroup unless the counts surprise us. One thing I want to check, though, is should we define replay exposure as event count, sequence strength, or something like total posterior mass? Those can behave pretty, pretty differently under the drift-only null, especially with the smoothing issue I saw in the last set.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Serrano
transcript.text: I’d resist choosing one of those as the exposure before we see how each one behaves against the behavioral endpoint. Event count is probably easiest for me to interpret, how often an item was revisited, but if strength or posterior mass is more stable under the drift null, that may be the defensible primary measure. Could we preregister one primary metric based on its null calibration, and keep the other two as converging analyses instead of letting whichever predicts error best win, and then...

transcript.speaker: Dr. Aaron Feldman
transcript.text: That’s the right way to choose it, not by which exposure happens to predict error best. I’d rank the three on calibration against the trajectory-label, circular-shift, and drift-only nulls, plus stability across a prespecified smoothing range. Then the primary is whichever survives that without inflating false sequences. I’m not yet sure whether posterior mass or, um, strength will win there, so we should leave the exact metric contingent on that preregistered calibration step.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Serrano
transcript.text: Okay, but I’d want that calibration step to be blind to the recall data, not just formally listed beforehand. Otherwise we’re still choosing a neural measure after seeing which one feels most plausible for the behavior. Could we freeze the metric based only on held-out recordings and those null results, and then bring in graded location error?

transcript.speaker: Dr. Aaron Feldman
transcript.text: That’s important. We can lock the choice using held-out recordings only. We assess calibration under the three null families, stability across the prespecified smoothing range, and maybe cross-validated predictive performance for the sequence model, all without loading any recall variables. I’ll need to spell out the tie-break rule, though, because I don’t want us quietly choosing between two adequately calibrated metrics after the fact.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Serrano
transcript.text: The tie-break needs to be mechanical enough that neither of us can reinterpret it later. Maybe calibration failure rules out a metric first, then among the survivors, we use the lowest held-out false-positive rate across the nulls, with a prespecified stability threshold. If they're still- if we still have a tie, we declare both primary rather than pick on intuition. Is that going to be feasible with the amount of held-out recording we expect?

transcript.speaker: Dr. Aaron Feldman
transcript.text: I think so, as long as we hold out blocks at the recording-session level, not by randomly splitting events, because otherwise correlated rest activity leaks across the split. The two-primary fallback is feasible, but I’d set it up so both, both have to pass the same calibration and stability criteria, and we report the multiplicity adjustment for the behavioral tests. I need to check the expected unit yields, though. That’s the limiting piece.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Serrano
transcript.text: Reserving whole recording blocks is non-negotiable if the rest activity is correlated. If unit yield means we can't support that split and the behavioral model, I'd rather simplify the neural claim than relax the holdout rule. Do you have even a rough sense, um, from the prior sessions how often we'd fall below that threshold?
